question: A UPS acceptance test includes:
choices: Static transfer from inverter to bypass and back
A vacuum-bottle pressure test
Tan delta of the battery jars only
Table 100.6 cable VLF in place of a function test
explanation: ATS 7.22.2 calls for the static transfer both ways, on normal load when you can. The pass criterion is the manufacturer’s data for that transfer, not a cable table.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.2

question: Automatic transfer switch control wiring shall not be less than:
choices: 2 MΩ
100 MΩ at 5 kV
The generator’s PI
explanation: 7.22.3.D.3 is 2 MΩ on control wiring. Power-contact microhms are a different line. The generator’s polarization index does not grade the transfer-switch wiring.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.D.3

question: An automatic transfer switch test is not finished when the relay picks up. ATS 7.22.3 also wants you to time:
choices: Delay on transfer, and delay plus retransfer when normal returns
Only the generator oil pressure
The fiber attenuation
The station battery specific gravity
explanation: The section lists time delay on transfer, the transfer itself, and time delay and retransfer when normal power returns. A contact closure in the test set does not prove the switch moved and came back.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3

question: During a UPS static-transfer test the inverter is the source and bypass is healthy. The test should show:
choices: Transfer to bypass and back, within the manufacturer’s time
That the bypass breaker is welded shut
A recloser vacuum test
Tan delta of the output cable instead of a transfer
explanation: ATS 7.22.2 wants the transfer both directions, preferably on real load, and the result compared with the UPS manual. A single transfer that never returns does not finish the test.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.2

question: A step-up transformer can be back-fed from the low-voltage side. Before a power-factor test you:
choices: Assume the LV bushings are dead because the HV breaker is open
Isolate and test both sides, because the LV side may be the source
Only ground the HV neutral
Skip LOTO if the nameplate says distribution
explanation: Opening the high side does not kill a unit fed from inverters, a generator, or another LV source. 29 CFR 1910.333 still wants every source disconnected, locked, and tested. Then the test voltage stays within the winding’s line-to-ground rating.
reference: 29 CFR 1910.333(b)(2); power-factor method, per Megger DELTA4000 applications guide

question: ATS 7.22.1.B.3 on an engine generator requires verification of:
choices: Phase rotation, phasing, and synchronized operation as the application requires
Only the oil dielectric strength
Zone 1 reach
A 30-minute VLF test of the stator
explanation: The generator has to land on the bus in the right rotation and in phase when the application needs that. The insulation-resistance test is a separate item, run in accordance with IEEE 43.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.3

question: ATS 7.22.1.B.6 calls for the engine-generator performance test to be run:
choices: In accordance with NFPA 110
As a 30-minute VLF test
Only if the polarization index fails
In place of the protective-shutdown tests
explanation: The performance test follows NFPA 110. The insulation-resistance test and the protective-shutdown tests are separate lines in the same section. Do not replace those with the performance run, or the other way around.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.6; NFPA 110-2025 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: NFPA 70B-2026 says maintenance information designates equipment as:
choices: Serviceable, limited-service, or nonserviceable
Pass, fail, or exempt from records
Class 1, 1A, or 2 only
Condition A or B
explanation: Those three words say what the equipment can still be used for. They are not the same as the condition score of 1, 2, or 3 that sets how often it is maintained.

question: NFPA 70B-2026 chapter 32 applies to a battery energy storage system above:
choices: 3.6 MJ, which is 1 kWh
50 kWh only
Any single flooded cell
A transfer switch
explanation: The storage-system chapter starts above 3.6 MJ, equal to 1 kWh. That energy number does not by itself pull every standby battery into the chapter. Section 32.1.2 lists the applications that stay outside it. When the manufacturer is silent, performance for a system that is in the chapter follows that chapter's interval table.

question: Which test is on the battery-energy-storage list in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 32.3.5 and would be the wrong list for a standby battery jar?
choices: Battery-management-system review, thermal survey, and ultrasonic inspection
Specific gravity of a flooded cell
Individual float voltage to two decimals
Connection resistance of a vented cell
explanation: The storage-system table includes a thermal survey, ultrasonic inspection, cable insulation resistance, connection resistance, a performance test, and a review of the battery-management system. Specific gravity and two-decimal float voltage are the stationary-standby chapter. A system at or below 1 kWh is not pulled into chapter 32 by the title alone.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, Table 32.3.5

question: NFPA 70B-2026 visual inspection of a transfer switch, conditions 1, 2, and 3, is:
choices: 12, 6, and 3 months
60, 36, and 12 months, the same as the electrical row
12, 12, and 6 months, the transformer-fluid row
Before each use
explanation: Visual inspection of transfer switches is 12, 6, and 3 months. The other transfer-switch tasks, when the manufacturer is silent, are 60, 36, and 12 months. Do not put the visual check on the grounding electrical-test row.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, 39.2 and Table 9.3.2

question: Which test is listed for a transfer switch in NFPA 70B-2026 Table 39.3.5?
choices: Insulation resistance, protective devices, operators, transfer sequence, bypass or isolation, and operation under load
Dissolved-gas analysis
Vacuum-interrupter integrity
A turns-ratio test of the switch
explanation: The transfer-switch electrical list is insulation resistance, protective devices, the operators, the transfer sequence, bypass or isolation when the switch has it, and operation under load. Oil tests and vacuum-bottle tests belong to other equipment. No transfer-time limit is printed.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, Table 39.3.5

question: A test that is NOT part of caring for a transfer switch under NFPA 70B-2026 Table 39.3.5 is:
choices: Operating the transfer under load
Proving the bypass or isolation mechanism when the switch has one
Functional transfer testing
A dissolved-gas analysis of the switch
explanation: The electrical list includes insulation resistance, protective devices, operators, functional transfer testing, bypass or isolation, and operation under load. Dissolved gas is a liquid-filled transformer test, not a transfer-switch test.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, Tables 39.3.5 and 39.3.1

question: When the manufacturer is silent, NFPA 70B-2026 Table 32.2 puts battery-energy-storage performance, conditions 1, 2, and 3, at:
choices: 36, 36, and 12 months
12, 12, and 1 month, the vented float-voltage row
24, 24, and 12 months, the valve-regulated cell performance row
Before each use
explanation: That performance row is for a storage system above 1 kWh. It is not the stationary-standby float-voltage interval and it is not the valve-regulated jar performance row. The storage tests are thermal, ultrasonic, cable insulation, connection resistance, performance, and a battery-management review. No kilowatt-hour pass limit is printed beyond the chapter threshold.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, Table 32.2

question: Servicing a transfer switch under NFPA 70B-2026 includes manual operation, bolted connections, and interlocks. Those are not the same item as:
choices: The electrical list of insulation resistance, operators, sequence, and operation under load
A job you may skip if the visual interval has not come due
Something the chapter assigns to a relay timing test
A dissolved-gas sample
explanation: Manual operation, bolted connections, and interlocks are the servicing checks. The electrical table then calls for insulation resistance, protective devices, operators, the transfer sequence, bypass or isolation, and operation under load. Visual inspection is still 12, 6, and 3 months. No operating-time limit is printed.
reference: NFPA 70B-2026, Tables 39.3.4 and 39.3.5

question: Which engine shutdowns does ATS 7.22.1 have you functionally test on a generator set?
choices: Low fuel tank level, ambient temperature, and humidity
Low oil pressure, overtemperature, and overspeed
Battery charger ripple and dc ground
Exhaust stack height and muffler noise
explanation: The safety shutdowns that protect the engine are proved by actually operating them: low oil pressure, overtemperature, and overspeed. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.4

question: During inspection of an automatic transfer switch, ATS 7.22.3 has you check manual transfer and also:
choices: That both sources can be closed together briefly to share load
That the neutral is bonded at the switch
That the generator is synchronized before each transfer
Positive mechanical interlocking between sources
explanation: The mechanical interlock must keep the two sources from being connected together. Manual transfer is checked along with it. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.A.9 and A.10.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.A.9 and A.10

question: On a UPS acceptance test, ATS 7.22.2 checks the dc undervoltage setting. When the dc falls to that level it should:
choices: Start the standby generator
Transfer the load to the maintenance bypass manually
Raise the charger to equalize voltage
Trip the inverter input breaker
explanation: The dc undervoltage trip protects the battery and inverter by opening the inverter input breaker. The level is set to the manufacturer's value. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.2.B.4 and D.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.2.B.4 and D.4

question: The normal source to an automatic transfer switch fails. In what order should the ATS operate? (ATS 7.22.3 has you verify each of these functions.)
choices: Transfer, engine start, alternate source sensed, delay on transfer
Normal sensing drops, engine starts, alternate sensed, delay, transfer
Engine start, transfer, normal-source sensing drops out, delay on transfer
Delay on retransfer, engine start, transfer, alternate sensed
explanation: ATS lists normal-source voltage and frequency sensing, engine start, time delay on transfer, alternate-source sensing, transfer, and then delay with retransfer and engine cooldown and shutdown when normal returns. That is a checklist, not the running order. In operation the transfer delay only finishes and the switch only moves once the alternate source is up and sensed good. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.B.8.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.B.8

question: Utility power returns after an outage. In the ATS 7.22.3 timing list, what follows the retransfer?
choices: An immediate engine stop at the instant of retransfer
Engine cooldown, then shutdown
A second transfer back to the generator
A battery equalize charge
explanation: After the retransfer delay and the retransfer, the engine runs unloaded for its cooldown period and then shuts down. Both times are verified. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.B.8.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.3.B.8

question: A 125 kW standby generator stator gives a 1-minute insulation test with a dielectric absorption ratio of 1.2. Under ATS 7.22.1:
choices: It fails, because the DAR must be at least 1.4
It needs a 10-minute PI test because of its size
It fails, because every generator must show a PI of 2.0 from a 1-minute test
It meets the DAR limit (above 1.0); check Table 100.11 too
explanation: Machines of 200 hp (150 kW) and below get a 1-minute test and a DAR, which must be greater than 1.0. Larger machines get a 10-minute test and a PI of at least 2.0. The 1.4 DAR figure is for induction motors under 7.15.1. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.1 and D.1.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025 7.22.1.B.1 and D.1

question: Emergency loads hang on a single feeder through one automatic transfer switch. What does NEC 700.5 add so the switch can be maintained?
choices: Nothing; the switch is taken out of service for maintenance
A second utility service only
A portable generator connection in place of the transfer switch
Redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation switch
explanation: 700.5(D) asks for redundant transfer equipment or a bypass-isolation switch when emergency loads are on a single feeder, so 700.3(C) maintenance can be done without losing the loads. 700.5(B) says bypass-isolation switches must prevent inadvertent paralleling. If the backup path is manual, a qualified person actively supervises it while the automatic switch is out. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.5(B) and (D).

question: Where does ATS 7.22.3 direct insulation-resistance testing of a transfer switch?
choices: Every pole with the switch in each source position, plus across open poles
Phase-to-ground only, with the switch in the normal position
Only across the closed contacts
Control wiring only, at 2,500 V dc
explanation: B.2 covers both source positions and across each open pole. Control wiring is a separate item at 500 V dc for 300 V cable or 1,000 V dc for 600 V cable, with 2 MΩ minimum. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.2, B.3 and D.3.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.2, B.3 and D.3

question: Contact resistance across the poles of a transfer switch reads 42, 45 and 66 µΩ. With no manufacturer's range, what does ATS say?
choices: Accept all three: they are under 100 µΩ
Investigate the 45 µΩ pole, since it differs from the 42 µΩ pole
Investigate the 66 µΩ pole: it is more than 50% above the lowest value
Investigate only if a pole exceeds twice the average
explanation: Without manufacturer data, ATS compares poles and flags any that deviate by more than 50% of the lowest. 42 × 1.5 = 63 µΩ, so 66 µΩ is over and 45 µΩ is not. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.4 and D.4.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.4 and D.4

question: How does NEC 700.5(C) require an automatic transfer switch for an emergency system to be operated and held?
choices: Manually operated and electrically held
Electrically operated and electrically held
Electrically operated and mechanically held
Spring operated with no holding means
explanation: An emergency ATS must be electrically operated and mechanically held. The holding is mechanical, not dependent on a coil staying energized. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.5(C).

question: Under the NEC, an emergency-system transfer switch must be:
choices: Automatic, listed for emergency use, and unable to interconnect the sources
Manual, so a qualified person on site decides every single transfer
Shared with standby loads so the generator stays loaded
Reconditioned equipment, if it passes a functional test
explanation: 700.5 requires automatic, listed, emergency-marked transfer equipment that cannot interconnect the sources by accident. It supplies only emergency loads. Reconditioned transfer switches are not allowed. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.5(A) and (E); 700.2.

question: Under NEC 700.12, how quickly must an emergency system supply power after normal power fails?
choices: Within 60 seconds
Within 5 minutes, measured from the generator reaching rated speed
There is no time limit; it depends only on the generator
Within the time required for the application, but not more than 10 seconds
explanation: 700.12 caps emergency systems at 10 seconds. Legally required standby under 701.12 gets 60 seconds. The project specification can be stricter, so check it too. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.12 and 701.12.

question: Normal power comes back for only a moment during a test, and the emergency transfer switch should not run straight back to normal. Which NEC feature is that?
choices: An in-phase monitor on the alternate source
A time delay that rides through a brief return of normal power
An elevator pre-signal contact that warns the elevator controller
A load-shed contact that drops nonessential loads
explanation: 700.12 calls for a time delay so that a short return of normal power does not cause a retransfer. ATS 7.22.3 has you time the retransfer delay against the design during the functional test. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.12(D)(1); ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.8.

question: Who witnesses the commissioning test of an NEC Article 700 emergency system, and what must be kept afterward?
choices: The generator vendor only, with no written record required
The AHJ witnesses it, and a written test and maintenance record is kept
The serving utility, which keeps the records in its own files
The electrical inspector only if a failure occurs
explanation: 700.3 has the AHJ witness the test on installation and periodically, sets periodic tests on an approved schedule, requires maintenance, and requires a written record of tests and maintenance. Source: NFPA 70-2023 (NEC), 700.3(A)-(D).

question: On a transfer switch functional test, the engine-start, transfer, retransfer and cooldown delays all operate. How do you judge the measured times?
choices: Against a fixed NETA table of seconds for each delay
Against the previous technician's notes only
Any time under 60 seconds passes for every delay in the sequence
Against the manufacturer's data and design settings, within NFPA 110 minimums
explanation: ATS 7.22.3.D.8 sends you to the manufacturer and the system design; ATS itself has no table of seconds. NFPA 110 sets floors for operational-test settings: start delay at least 1 s, return to normal at least 5 min, shutdown at least 5 min, and no minimum on transfer to emergency. Record each setting and each measured time so the next test can compare. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.D.8; NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.5.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.D.8; NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.5 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Besides the timing list, which two electrical items does ATS 7.22.3 add for a transfer switch's controls and sources?
choices: Relays and timers set per Section 7.9, and phase rotation and phasing verified
Measure turns ratio and excitation current on the switch's control transformer
Run a VLF withstand on the load cables in both source positions
Perform a dissolved-gas analysis of the switch
explanation: B.6 sends relays and timers to Section 7.9. B.7 checks that both sources have matching rotation and phasing, plus synchronized operation where the application uses it. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.6 and B.7.
reference: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.3.B.6 and B.7

question: An emergency power supply system is designated Type 10, Class 2. What does that mean under NFPA 110?
choices: 10 h of fuel at rated load, and transfer within 2 s
Level 1 service with a 10-minute cooldown and 2 transfer switches
Power restored at the ATS load terminals within 10 s, and at least 2 h at rated load without refueling
A 10 kW unit able to carry 2 times its rating briefly
explanation: Type is the longest allowed loss of power at the transfer-switch load terminals: Type 10 means 10 seconds. Class is the minimum time, in hours, the system runs at rated load without refueling or recharging, so Class 2 is 2 hours. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 4.1 to 4.3 and Tables 4.1(a) and 4.1(b).
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 4.1 to 4.3 and Tables 4.1(a) and 4.1(b) (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: An EPSS is listed as Class 0.083. About how long must it carry rated load without refueling?
choices: 5 minutes
8.3 minutes
15 minutes
83 minutes
explanation: Class is in hours. 0.083 h × 60 ≈ 5 minutes. Class 0.25 is 15 minutes. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 4.2 and Table 4.1(a).
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 4.2 and Table 4.1(a) (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A 500 kW standby diesel is exercised monthly under NFPA 110 using the nameplate-load criterion. What minimum load and run time apply?
choices: At least 250 kW (50%) for 15 minutes
At least 500 kW (100%) for 60 minutes
Any load for at least 10 minutes
At least 150 kW (30% of nameplate) for at least 30 minutes
explanation: Monthly exercise is at least 30 minutes under load. For a diesel, the load either reaches the manufacturer's minimum exhaust temperature or is at least 30% of the standby kW rating: 0.30 × 500 = 150 kW. A load bank can make up the difference. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.2 and 8.4.2.1.1 to 8.4.2.1.2.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.2 and 8.4.2.1.1 to 8.4.2.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: How often does NFPA 110 require each automatic transfer switch to be operated, and how?
choices: Annually, by hand with the maintenance handle
Monthly, electrically transferring from the primary to the alternate source and back
Every 36 months during the Level 1 test only
Weekly, by pressing the lamp test button
explanation: Each ATS is electrically operated from primary to alternate and back every month. The Type time limit doesn't have to be met on that monthly operation, but there has to be a way to confirm compliance once a year. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.6 to 8.4.6.2.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.6 to 8.4.6.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: For an operational test of a generator EPSS, which delay settings match NFPA 110 minimums?
choices: Start delay at least 10 s, retransfer at least 1 min, cooldown not required
Start delay at least 1 s, retransfer to normal at least 5 min, and shutdown (cooldown) at least 5 min
Transfer to emergency at least 5 min, with no minimum on retransfer
All delays set to zero so the test runs fast
explanation: NFPA 110 sets floors of 1 s on the start delay (0.5 s for gas turbines), 5 min on restoration to normal, and 5 min on shutdown. Transfer to emergency has no minimum. The 5-minute cooldown is waived for small air-cooled engines, 15 kW and under. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.5 and 6.2.10 to 6.2.10.2.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.5 and 6.2.10 to 6.2.10.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: An 800 kW generator is on its acceptance test. After the initial 1.5-hour run, what does the 2-hour load test require?
choices: 800 kW for the full 2 hours with no steps
400 kW for 60 min, then 800 kW for 60 min
240 kW for 2 hours
At least 240 kW for 30 min, then at least 400 kW for 30 min, then 800 kW for 60 min
explanation: The full-load test runs at 30%, then 50% for 30 minutes each, then full load for 60 minutes, with site derating applied: 0.3 × 800 = 240 kW, 0.5 × 800 = 400 kW, then 800 kW. A load bank can supplement building load, and coolant temperature must be stable for at least the last 30 minutes. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 7.13.4.5.1 to 7.13.4.5.4.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 7.13.4.5.1 to 7.13.4.5.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A 600 kW diesel can't meet the monthly exhaust-temperature or 30% load criteria on building load. What annual test does NFPA 110 add?
choices: At least 300 kW for 30 min, then at least 450 kW for 60 min, continuously (1.5 h total)
600 kW for 4 hours
180 kW for 30 min once a year
No annual test; monthly runs on available load are enough
explanation: A diesel that falls short of the monthly criteria keeps its monthly runs on available load and adds a yearly supplemental test: at least 50% of nameplate kW for 30 minutes, then at least 75% for 60 minutes, without stopping. 0.5 × 600 = 300 kW and 0.75 × 600 = 450 kW. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.2.4.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.2.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A Level 1 EPSS is rated Class 6. How long must its 36-month test run under NFPA 110?
choices: 6 continuous hours, no exceptions
1.5 hours, the same as acceptance
4 continuous hours, since termination at 4 h is allowed when the Class exceeds 4 h
30 minutes, the same as the monthly exercise
explanation: At least every 36 months, a Level 1 EPSS is run continuously for its Class duration. When the Class is longer than 4 hours, the test may stop after 4 continuous hours: min(6, 4) = 4 h. A diesel carries at least 30% of nameplate kW or enough load for the manufacturer's minimum exhaust temperature. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.9 to 8.4.9.7.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 8.4.9 to 8.4.9.7 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A generator's failure could kill or badly hurt someone at this site. Which NFPA 110 level applies, and how often is it inspected?
choices: Level 2, inspected monthly
Level 1, inspected monthly
Level 1, inspected weekly
Level 2, inspected weekly
explanation: Level 1 is for systems whose failure could kill or badly hurt someone, and its equipment is inspected weekly. Level 2 covers less critical loads and gets at least a monthly visual inspection. Both levels are exercised under load at least monthly. Source: NFPA 110-2025, 4.4.1 to 4.4.2 and 8.4.1.1 to 8.4.1.2.
reference: NFPA 110-2025, 4.4.1 to 4.4.2 and 8.4.1.1 to 8.4.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A building uses the manual testing option for its battery emergency lights under NFPA 101. What does the monthly functional test look like?
choices: Each unit runs on battery for 90 minutes every month
Each unit runs for 5 minutes once every 60 days
Each unit runs on battery for at least 30 seconds, with tests spaced 3 to 5 weeks apart
The test button is pressed once a year for 30 seconds
explanation: The short check is at least 30 seconds of operation, done monthly, and the gap between tests must fall between 3 and 5 weeks. The long 1.5-hour run is the annual test for battery units. Keep written records for the AHJ. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.1.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: How long is the annual test on battery-powered emergency lighting under NFPA 101?
choices: At least 1.5 hours
At least 30 minutes
At least 4 hours
At least 24 hours
explanation: Battery emergency lights get a yearly discharge of at least an hour and a half, which matches the required emergency lighting duration. The lights must keep working the whole time. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.1.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: After normal lighting fails, how long must NFPA 101 emergency illumination keep going?
choices: At least 10 seconds, until the generator picks up
At least 30 minutes
At least 8 hours
At least 1.5 hours
explanation: Emergency illumination is required for at least 90 minutes after normal lighting is lost. That is why the battery test is 90 minutes and why a generator serving these loads needs at least Class 1.5. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: At the start of an emergency lighting test, an egress path averages 1.3 foot-candles, but one spot reads 0.08 foot-candle. What is the result?
choices: It passes, because the average is above 1 foot-candle
It fails, because no point may start below 0.1 foot-candle even when the average is good
It passes, because the end-of-test minimum is 0.06 foot-candle
It fails, because the average must start at 5 foot-candles
explanation: At the start, the path needs both an average of at least 1 foot-candle and no point under 0.1 foot-candle. A good average does not cover a dark spot. The lower 0.6 average and 0.06 minimum figures only apply at the end of the 1.5 hours. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.1 to 7.9.2.1.2.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.1 to 7.9.2.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: At the end of the 1.5-hour run, the same path averages 0.7 foot-candle with a lowest point of 0.07. Is that acceptable under NFPA 101?
choices: No. The starting values of 1.0 average and 0.1 minimum must hold the whole time
Yes. Light may decline to an average of at least 0.6 and a minimum of at least 0.06 foot-candle by the end
No. The average must never drop below 0.9
Yes, because only the average matters at the end
explanation: NFPA 101 allows the light to fade during the run. At the end, the floor of the path may be down to an average of 0.6 foot-candle and a lowest point of 0.06. Both readings here sit just above those floors. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.2.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: On an egress path, the brightest emergency reading is 5.0 foot-candles and the dimmest is 0.1. What does NFPA 101 say about that spread?
choices: It passes, since both readings meet the minimum
It passes, since the limit is 100 to 1
It fails because the brightest spot is over 1 foot-candle
It fails the uniformity limit: 5.0 / 0.1 = 50, and the maximum-to-minimum ratio may not exceed 40 to 1
explanation: NFPA 101 also limits how uneven the lighting can be. Divide the highest reading by the lowest: 5.0 / 0.1 = 50. That is above the 40 to 1 limit, so the layout or aiming needs work even though the minimum is met. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.3.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.1.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Emergency lights with self-testing, self-diagnostic batteries are installed. Under that NFPA 101 option, what does the owner still have to do?
choices: Visually inspect at least every 30 days and run an annual test of at least 1.5 hours, with written records
Nothing. The units test themselves, so no visits or records are needed
Only replace the batteries every 5 years
Run a 30-second manual test every week
explanation: The units handle their own 30-second check every 30 days and show a failure. People still have to look at them at least every 30 days and run the yearly 90-minute test, and the results get written down. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.2.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.3.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A new generator will power required emergency lighting. Under NFPA 101, what is the minimum NFPA 110 rating for that system?
choices: Type 60, Class 2, Level 2
Type 10, Class 24, Level 2
Type 10, Class 1.5, Level 1
Type 120, Class 1.5, Level 1
explanation: New emergency power for egress lighting has to restore power within 10 seconds (Type 10), carry the load for at least 1.5 hours (Class 1.5), and be held to Level 1, the life-safety level. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.2.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.9.2.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: An exit sign is lit by a separate fixture shining on it. What minimum light on the sign face does NFPA 101 call for?
choices: 1 foot-candle (10.8 lux)
0.1 foot-candle (1.1 lux)
5 foot-candles (54 lux), with a contrast ratio of at least 0.5
50 foot-candles (540 lux)
explanation: Externally lit signs must get 5 foot-candles or more on the face and enough contrast, 0.5 or better, to be read. Internally lit signs are a different path: they are listed to UL 924. Source: NFPA 101-2027, 7.10.6.3 and 7.10.7.1.
reference: NFPA 101-2027, 7.10.6.3 and 7.10.7.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A stored-energy system is rated Type A under NFPA 111. What is the longest loss of power allowed at the transfer switch load terminals?
choices: One quarter cycle (about 0.0042 s)
One full cycle (about 0.0167 s)
10 seconds
No time limit
explanation: NFPA 111 types are named by the allowed gap. Type O has none, Type A is a quarter cycle, Type B is one cycle, Type 10 is 10 seconds, and Type M is manual with no limit. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 4.2.1 and Table 4.2.2.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 4.2.1 and Table 4.2.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A UPS feeding emergency loads is NFPA 111 Class 0.25. How long must it carry rated load without recharging?
choices: 25 minutes
2.5 minutes
2.5 hours
15 minutes
explanation: Class is in hours: 0.25 h × 60 = 15 minutes. The other fixed classes: Class 0.033 runs 2 minutes, 0.083 runs 5, and 1.5 runs 90. Class X is a time set by the application. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 4.3 and Table 4.3.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 4.3 and Table 4.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: During the NFPA 111 acceptance test of a battery-based system, how is the normal power failure simulated?
choices: Pull one battery jumper so the charger alarms
Open the normal-supply switches or breakers with all emergency loads connected, then record transfer time, load voltage and load current
Press the UPS self-test button and read the screen
Unplug the inverter control power and watch it reboot
explanation: The test starts with charged batteries and a rated load. Normal power is cut by opening its own disconnects, and every emergency load is on, including ones that are normally dead. Write down how long the system took to pick up the load, plus voltage, current and, where it applies, frequency. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.2.1.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.2.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Right after the first NFPA 111 acceptance run, what happens before the full-class load test?
choices: The batteries are replaced with new ones
The system goes back on normal power for 24 hours to recharge
The full-class test starts at once without recharging
The system is left off for a week to rest the cells
explanation: After the first run, the system is reconnected to normal power for a day. Then it is tested at full load for its whole Class time. A load bank equal to the equipment rating may make up any missing site load. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.2.2 to 7.6.2.3.3.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.2.2 to 7.6.2.3.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A Class 1.5 stored-energy system gets its annual NFPA 111 load test. Which of these meets the requirement?
choices: 100% of rated load for 90 minutes and 60% load for 90 minutes, both every year
60% of rated load for 54 minutes
Any load for 15 minutes
100% of rated load for 54 minutes, or 60% of rated load for the full 90 minutes
explanation: The annual test is one of two options: full load for 60% of the Class time, or 60% load for all of it. Class 1.5 is 90 minutes, so 0.6 × 90 = 54 minutes at full load, or 90 minutes at 60% load. You pick one, not both. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 8.4.4.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 8.4.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A battery-based Class 1.5 system just ran a full 90-minute outage. What recharge does NFPA 111 expect?
choices: 80% within 18 hours (12 × the 1.5 h discharge) and 100% within 48 hours
100% within 1 hour
80% within 1.5 hours and 100% within 12 hours
No recharge limit is given
explanation: Battery systems with a matched charger must reach 80% charge in no more than 12 × the discharge time: 12 × 1.5 h = 18 h. Full charge must come back within 48 hours. The 1-hour figure applies to ultracapacitor and flywheel-type systems. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 5.2.8.2.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 5.2.8.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A lead-acid battery in a stored-energy system has permanent ohmic monitoring. When are the NFPA 111 baseline readings on every cell taken?
choices: During the acceptance discharge, at the lowest voltage
Only when a cell fails
Fully charged on float, about half a year past the full-load test; if it has been discharged since, 2 weeks after that discharge
On the day the battery is delivered, before it is charged
explanation: The baseline comes after the battery has settled: roughly half a year after the full-load test, or two weeks following the latest discharge. The battery must be fully charged and on float. Later readings are compared with this baseline. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.5 to 7.6.5.1.2.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 7.6.5 to 7.6.5.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A routine ohmic check on a stored-energy battery shows a deviation from baseline that the program calls unacceptable. What does NFPA 111 require next?
choices: Nothing until the next annual test
Equalize the battery and repeat the ohmic reading only
A load test for the full Class duration
Replace the charger
explanation: Ohmic readings are a screen. When the deviation from baseline is unacceptable, the next step is a full-Class-duration load test to find out what the battery can really do. A load bank equal to the equipment rating may stand in for the actual load. Source: NFPA 111-2025, 8.4.3.2 to 8.4.3.2.2.
reference: NFPA 111-2025, 8.4.3.2 to 8.4.3.2.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: How often does NFPA 99 require the on-site generator serving a hospital essential electrical system to be tested?
choices: 12 times a year, with 20 to 40 days between tests
Once a year
Every week
Every 36 months only
explanation: The on-site sources are tested a dozen times a year. No gap between tests may be shorter than 20 days or longer than 40. Generators follow NFPA 110 Chapter 8 for how the test is done. Source: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.1.5(A).
reference: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.1.5(A) (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Under NFPA 99, how fast must the life safety and critical branches be back on after a power loss?
choices: Within 60 seconds
Within 5 minutes, after the equipment branch
Manually, when an operator gets there
Automatically within 10 seconds
explanation: Both the life safety and the critical branch must be re-energized automatically in 10 seconds or less. The equipment branch is allowed to follow later, on a delay. Source: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.5.3.1.
reference: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.5.3.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: During a monthly hospital generator test, power reaches the critical branch in 12 seconds. What does NFPA 99 say?
choices: The generator fails and must be taken out of service at once
The 10-second limit doesn't apply to the monthly test, but the facility must have a process to confirm 10-second capability every year
Nothing; timing is never checked
The monthly test must be repeated until it hits 10 seconds
explanation: The 10-second restoration target isn't enforced on the monthly run, since it is a planned test. If it isn't met, the facility needs a set way to show once a year that the system can do it. Source: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.1.2(A) to (B).
reference: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.1.2(A) to (B) (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Which hospital EES branch is allowed to come back on a delay after the life safety and critical branches?
choices: The life safety branch
The equipment branch
The critical branch
None; all three must close at once
explanation: The equipment branch picks up its loads automatically after a delay, or by hand in sequence, so the generator isn't overloaded. The life safety and critical branches are fed first. Source: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.5.1.4.2(A) and 6.7.3.4.1.
reference: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.5.1.4.2(A) and 6.7.3.4.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: When does NFPA 99 call for insulation resistance readings on the main feeders of the essential electrical system?
choices: Every month with the generator test
Only if a breaker trips
Never; only the generator windings are tested
Before acceptance, and any time damage is suspected
explanation: The main feeders get an insulation resistance test before the system is accepted, and again whenever there is reason to think they were damaged. Source: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.2.1.
reference: NFPA 99-2027, 6.7.4.1.2.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Using NFPA 99 Table 6.9.4.1, what schedule applies to hospital transfer equipment?
choices: Inspect monthly; service and test every 3 years
Inspect yearly; test every 5 years
Inspect weekly; test monthly
No schedule; follow NFPA 110 only
explanation: The table puts transfer equipment on a monthly inspection with service and testing on a 3-year cycle. For generators, the table defers to NFPA 110 Chapter 8. Check the whole table and its notes for other equipment and allowed changes. Source: NFPA 99-2027, Table 6.9.4.1.
reference: NFPA 99-2027, Table 6.9.4.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: On a protected-premises fire alarm system, how quickly must the secondary supply take over when primary voltage is inadequate?
choices: Within 60 seconds
Within 5 minutes
Automatically within 10 seconds
Manually, after the trouble signal is answered
explanation: The secondary supply has to pick up on its own within 10 seconds, and required signals can't be lost or delayed by more than 10 seconds. The 60-second figure applies to supervising-station facilities. Source: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.6.1 to 10.6.6.3.
reference: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.6.1 to 10.6.6.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: What standby capacity does NFPA 72 require from the secondary supply of a protected-premises fire alarm system (no voice system)?
choices: 4 hours of standby, then 15 minutes of alarm
90 minutes of standby and alarm
24 hours of normal standby, then 5 minutes of alarm
8 hours of standby, then 1 hour of alarm
explanation: The secondary supply carries the system quiet for a full day, then runs the alarm notification for 5 minutes. Count every load that isn't shed automatically on transfer when sizing the battery. Source: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.7.2.1 to 10.6.7.2.2 and 10.6.7.2.13.
reference: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.7.2.1 to 10.6.7.2.2 and 10.6.7.2.13 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: An in-building emergency voice/alarm system is being checked for battery size. What capacity must the secondary supply have?
choices: 24 hours of quiescent load, then 15 minutes of emergency operation at maximum connected load
24 hours, then 5 minutes of alarm
1.5 hours of emergency operation
15 minutes of standby only
explanation: Voice systems keep the same 24-hour quiet period but need 15 minutes of emergency operation afterward, at the full connected load, instead of the 5 minutes used for a plain alarm. Source: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.7.2.3 to 10.6.7.2.4.
reference: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.7.2.3 to 10.6.7.2.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A generator provides the secondary power for a protected-premises fire alarm system. What NFPA 110 rating does NFPA 72 require?
choices: Type 60, Class 24, Level 2
Type 10, Class 1.5, Level 1
Type 120, Class 2, Level 2
Type 10, Class 24, Level 1
explanation: The generator must restore power in 10 seconds and run 24 hours, at Level 1. An automatic-start generator at a supervising station is held to Type 60, Class 24, Level 2. Source: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.11.3.1.1 to 10.6.11.3.2.1.
reference: NFPA 72-2025, 10.6.11.3.1.1 to 10.6.11.3.2.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: During the annual secondary-power test on a fire alarm panel, what does NFPA 72 have you do after removing primary power?
choices: Leave primary off for 24 hours before checking anything
Confirm the trouble signal, check the battery against the load with margin, then run the general alarm at least 5 minutes (voice at least 15)
Disconnect the batteries too and watch for a reboot
Only read the panel's battery voltage display
explanation: With primary off, the panel should show trouble. Measure or confirm the standby and alarm current against the manufacturer's data and the battery rating, with a safety margin. Run the alarm for at least 5 minutes, or 15 for voice, then restore primary. Source: NFPA 72-2025, Table 14.4.3.2 item 8.
reference: NFPA 72-2025, Table 14.4.3.2 item 8 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A fire pump controller is rated 480 V. Under NFPA 20, what is the lowest voltage allowed at its line terminals while the motor starts?
choices: 456 V (5% below)
408 V (no more than 15% below rated)
384 V (20% below)
432 V (10% below)
explanation: During starting, the controller line terminals may sag no more than 15% below the controller's rated voltage: 480 × 0.85 = 408 V. The tighter 5% limit is at the motor contactor load terminals when running at 115% of full-load current. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 9.4.1 to 9.4.3.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 9.4.1 to 9.4.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A 460 V fire pump motor runs at 115% of its full-load current. What is the lowest NFPA 20 voltage at the motor contactor load terminals?
choices: 391 V (15% below)
414 V (10% below)
460 V (no drop allowed)
437 V (no more than 5% below the motor rating)
explanation: With the motor drawing 115% of full-load amps, the contactor's load-side terminals can sit no more than 5% under the motor's rated voltage: 460 × 0.95 = 437 V. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 9.4.4.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 9.4.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: At fire pump acceptance, voltage is checked at the motor contactor output lugs on a 460 V motor. What band does NFPA 20 allow?
choices: 437 V to 506 V (5% below to 10% above nameplate)
414 V to 483 V
391 V to 529 V
455 V to 465 V
explanation: During the field test, the voltage at the contactor output lugs can be as low as 5% under or as high as 10% over the nameplate: 0.95 × 460 = 437 V and 1.10 × 460 = 506 V. Each phase current must also stay at or under service-factor amps. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.6.7.1 to 14.2.6.7.3.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.6.7.1 to 14.2.6.7.3 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: How many controller operations does an NFPA 20 acceptance test require on an electric fire pump?
choices: One automatic start and one manual stop
3 automatic and 3 manual, 1 minute each
At least 6 automatic and 6 manual, with the pump at full speed at least 5 minutes each time
12 automatic only, no run time
explanation: The controller is cycled at least six times automatically and six times by hand, following the manufacturer's procedure. On constant-speed electric pumps, each start is held at full speed for 5 minutes or more. Variable-speed pumps are exempt from the minimum run time. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.7.1 to 14.2.7.3.1.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.7.1 to 14.2.7.3.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: The fire pump has an alternate source and a transfer switch. In acceptance testing, how many of the controller operations must be done on the alternate source?
choices: Just one
None; the alternate source is tested separately under NFPA 110 only
At least half of the manual and automatic operations
All of them
explanation: NFPA 20 wants the alternate source proved under real starts, so at least half of the operations run on it. Normal power loss is also simulated at peak pump load to start the generator, where there is one, and transfer. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.8.1 to 14.2.8.4.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.8.1 to 14.2.8.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: While testing fire pump transfer and retransfer at peak load, the alternate feeder breaker trips. What does NFPA 20 say?
choices: That is a failure. Transfer and retransfer must not open the overcurrent devices in either line
That is normal, since inrush is expected
It passes if the normal side held
It only matters on a diesel pump
explanation: A transfer under full pump load must not trip the overcurrent protection on the normal or the alternate side. A trip means the protection, the sizing or the transfer timing needs to be fixed before acceptance. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.8.1 to 14.2.8.4.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.8.1 to 14.2.8.4 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Which kind of transfer switch is NOT allowed between the normal and alternate supplies of an electric fire pump?
choices: A listed fire-pump transfer switch
An electrically operated, mechanically held switch
A switch rated 115% or more of motor full-load amps
A manual transfer switch
explanation: NFPA 20 bans a manual transfer switch between the two supplies. The required switch is fire-pump listed and fault-current rated, operates electrically and latches mechanically, carries 115% or more of motor full-load amps, and can switch locked-rotor current. A manual operating means is still provided on it. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 10.8.1.2 and 10.8.3.1 to 10.8.3.5.1.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 10.8.1.2 and 10.8.3.1 to 10.8.3.5.1 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A fire pump motor is rated 460 V. Below what voltage on any normal-source phase must the transfer switch start the generator and transfer under NFPA 20?
choices: 391 V (85% of motor-rated voltage)
explanation: When any phase of the normal source drops below 85% of the motor's rated voltage, the transfer switch starts the standby generator, where there is one, and transfers: 460 × 0.85 = 391 V. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 10.8.3.6.2.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 10.8.3.6.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Besides the controller starts, which electrical check does NFPA 20 add at fire pump acceptance?
choices: A hipot of the motor at 2 × rated + 1000 V
A phase reversal test on the normal source and on the alternate source, where provided
A power factor test of the controller
A ground resistance test of the pump base
explanation: A fire pump that spins backward moves no water. Phase reversal is tested on each source, normal and alternate, where it is provided. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.6.12.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.6.12 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: Across all the NFPA 20 acceptance tests, what is the minimum total time the fire pump must run?
choices: 5 minutes
15 minutes
24 hours
1 hour
explanation: Add up the run time from every test step, including the alarm and signal checks. The total must be at least an hour. Source: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.10 to 14.2.11.
reference: NFPA 20-2025, 14.2.10 to 14.2.11 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: In an IT equipment room, a UPS sits inside the room. What must the NFPA 75 power disconnect do to it?
choices: Disconnect the UPS from its supply and also disconnect the battery from the load
Only shut off the input breaker
Only open the bypass
Nothing; UPS units are exempt at any size
explanation: The room disconnect has to kill power to the electronic equipment, including the UPS output fed from batteries. Opening the input alone leaves the load fed from the battery. Small sources, 750 VA or less, have an exception. Source: NFPA 75-2024, 11.4.5.1 and 11.5.1 to 11.5.1.2.
reference: NFPA 75-2024, 11.4.5.1 and 11.5.1 to 11.5.1.2 (background: not on the ETT reference list)

question: A UPS is being accepted. Inverter output looks clean on a meter, but no one has tested static transfer from the inverter to bypass and back. What should you require?
choices: A clean inverter voltage reading is enough to accept the static switch
Static transfer is only tested from bypass to inverter, never the reverse
UPS static-transfer tests are optional and may be left for the first outage
Test static transfer from the inverter to bypass and back, using normal load if possible, and confirm that the static transfer works the way the manufacturer specifies
explanation: ATS requires a static-transfer test from the inverter to bypass and back, using normal load if possible, and requires the static transfer to work the way the manufacturer specifies. A waveform check on the inverter does not prove the transfer path. Source: ANSI/NETA ATS-2025, 7.22.2.B.2 and 7.22.2.D.2.
